newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Veba offers C&W way out.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Veba offers C&W way out.

text.p: British telecommunications group Cable and Wireless and Veba AG on Tuesday seemed only to be discussing the terms of their divorce as senior executives discussed the impending break-up of their strategic alliance.

A high-ranking Veba official told reporters that the German utility has made C&W an offer to buy its 45 percent stake in their telecommunications venture Vebacom GmbH and that Veba was already searching for a new international partner.
"I am fairly certain that Cable and Wireless is going to leave," the Veba official said. "Basically it is regrettable that with this decision an international partner is leaving."

Veba made the offer over a week ago, the official said, adding that C&W did not have "all that long" to decide. Once accepted, the German utility would turn the stake over to a trustee in the hope of later transferring it to a new partner.
"We want to have an international partner and think it would be sensible for this to be an American partner," he added, but declined to elaborate on any of the prospects.
Veba would not comment on the statements.
When asked about the talks, a Veba spokeswoman said only that the company was speaking to many companies and there were a number of companies interested in the venture.
Industry sources said newspaper reports that U.S. regional phone company SBC Communications was likely to step in were "somewhat off the mark".

The statements come after days of speculation over the future of one of the most potent rivals gearing up to challenge German telecoms monopoly Deutsche Telekom AG when European telecoms markets are opened to competition next year.
Veba and Cable and Wireless first agreed on a strategic alliance in 1995. Veba took a 10.4 percent stake in the British company and won a seat on the board.

Last year, they agreed to bring German utility RWE AG on board, which would have reduced C&W's holdings to around 22 percent in the new company. But after the final contract was drawn up last month, C&W declined to sign it.

Under the terms of what the official called a "fair offer" made to C&W, the German utility would retain its C&W stake as an investment but would give up its board seat, which was linked to their alliance. Veba paid 2.2 billion marks for the stake, which is now worth around three billion marks.
Veba and RWE plan to move ahead with their plans to merge their telecommunications activities. "Everything is fine with RWE," the Veba official said.
The developments highlight the fluid nature of alliances in the sector as companies continually reassess strategies in an industry driven by rapid regulatory and technology changes.

Industry sources in London said Cable and Wireless had begun to fear it would not have enough management control and that the scale of investment required would make it difficult for the group to carry out needed expansion in its home market.

It must focus on its Cable and Wireless Communications consortium, which consists of a merger in Britain of its Mercury Communications unit and cable television operators NYNEX Cable Communications, Bell Cablemedia and Videotron.

While saying he was not privy to C&W's current moves, the Veba official said it was unlikely the British company would tie up with the Global One venture of Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom and Sprint Corp as widely believed.
"That does not really fit into the concept," he said.

Speaking to reporters in Munich, Global One chief executive Viesturs Vucins would not be drawn on questions about talks with C&W. "No comment," he told reporters when asked about press reports the two companies were talking.
The German government also took another step on Tuesday to spur competition in Europe's largest telecommunications market, expected to be worth some 100 billion marks by the year 2000.
It awarded the country's fourth mobile telephone licence to a E2 Mobilfunk GmbH consortium owned by British Telecom and German utility Viag AG .
Separately, a German government official told a conference that Bonn did not have the power to force Deutsche Telekom to sell its cable television network to promote competition.
The European Commission is studying ways to force telecoms monopolies to open their cable TV networks and there has been speculation that Telekom could be forced to sell its network.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, speaking in Hamburg, said he planned to take a close look this year at how EU states were dropping barriers to competition.
"Even after the opening of telecommunications market it must be prevented that the market dominance of former monopolies closes the door that has just been opened," he said.
